🤖 THREEHALVES — THE CENTAUR ROBOT Threehalves is a 7-foot-tall teleoperated robot developed by Satyress. Its design combines a human-like torso and arms with a powerful four-legged chassis, creating a mechanical centaur built for environments that are too dangerous for humans. The idea behind Threehalves is simple: instead of sending a person into extreme heat, unstable terrain, darkness, hazardous industrial environments or disaster zones, a skilled operator can control the robot remotely and perform the work from a safer location. Unlike many humanoid robots, Threehalves is designed around tools and equipment that humans already use. Its modular limbs and quick-connect system allow it to be adapted for different tasks, while its four-legged platform provides stability on difficult terrain. The most unsettling part is probably its appearance. With its enormous size, humanoid body, four mechanical legs and distinctive horned head, Threehalves looks less like a traditional industrial machine and more like something from a science-fiction horror movie. But behind the terrifying design is a serious engineering concept: putting the machine in danger instead of the human. Threehalves is still a developing robotics project, but it represents a strange glimpse into a future where dangerous jobs could be performed remotely — with a human controlling the machine from a distance. And honestly… it might be one of the creepiest robots ever built. 👁️ #threehalves #robot #baal #satyress #horrortok

Chinese humanoid robots broke records set by humans, including Usain Bolt's 100m sprint world record, on the opening day of the Olympics-like World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday. More than 2,000 humanoid robots were participating in the event, organisers said. In a 100-metre sprint, a humanoid robot achieved a result of 9.39 seconds, beating the human record of 9.58 seconds set by Jamaican athlete Bolt in 2009. In a standing high jump, a humanoid robot was able to reach 2.88m, well above the 0.95m best result by a humanoid in last year’s first edition of the games. It surpassed the human high jump record of 2.45m set by Cuba’s Javier Sotomayor in 1993. The five-day games, now in their second year, are a spectacle demonstrating China’s rapid progress in advanced robotics as the technology race with the US heats up. There are 51 events and more than 1,000 competitions taking place, including running, table tennis and football. For more news, visit @sbsnews_au (link in bio).

Visual artist Jason Cook  creates kinetic sculptures and robotic installations using electronics, programming and mechanical engineering. In The Walking Chair (2025), an ordinary wooden chair is transformed into a moving machine. A system of motors, mechanical parts and electronic components is attached beneath the seat, allowing the chair’s legs to move. By giving a familiar piece of furniture the ability to walk, Cook changes the way we perceive an everyday object. Sprout is Fauna Robotics’ small, developer-focused humanoid robot built to work safely around people in real-world spaces like labs, schools, offices, retail, and entertainment venues. It’s designed less like a shrunken factory robot and more like a “human-environment” platform: lightweight, padded/soft on the outside, and engineered to reduce impact risk with compliant control and limited joint torques. What makes Sprout interesting is the “full-stack” approach. Fauna positions it as a ready-to-build-on system where core capabilities—movement, perception, navigation, and social expression—work out of the box, so teams can spend time on applications instead of rebuilding fundamentals.  Sprout also leans into interaction: it can be directed via voice, has expressive features (like articulated eyebrows and LED facial elements), and supports things like whole-body control, grippers for manipulation, and even VR-based teleoperation within a unified hardware-software stack.  Pricing reported at launch is about $50,000, targeting researchers, universities, and builders who want a capable humanoid platform without starting from scratch.#ainews #robotics #Techtok #futuretech

videos.caption: Figure did something absolutely wild with its retired humanoid robots. 🤯🔥 Instead of dismantling its F.02 fleet, Figure trained the robots to autonomously jump into a 75-ton electric arc furnace filled with molten steel in Imatra, Finland. And yes this was real. Figure says the robots were: 🤖 Trained to jump in simulation 🦘 Practiced with airbags at its San Jose campus 🏭 Sent to a foundry the team had never visited 🔥 Given only six furnace melts across 24 hours ⚡ Operating despite extreme heat and electromagnetic interference The reason? Figure wanted to decommission the F.02 fleet while protecting proprietary hardware and freeing engineering resources for its next-generation robots. The resulting metal bars are being turned into a limited series of F.02 commemorative artifacts. And there is a serious robotics story behind the crazy video: Figure had to train a jump policy that could transfer from simulation to a completely unfamiliar real-world environment and accurately land the robot in the furnace. Arnold Schwarzenegger was also involved after suggesting the robots should be melted an obvious nod to Terminator 2. This may be the most brutal robot retirement ever. 😅 Would you call this engineering genius or the most extreme robot disposal method ever? 👀 🏢 Company: Figure , Brett Adcock ⚠️ This content is shared for informational purposes only. I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.

I'm sorry... but who looked at this and said, "Yep, that's the design!"? 🤣 If your rescue robot walks out of the woods looking like a seven-foot-tall mechanical demon carrying a chainsaw... maybe the branding department got a little carried away. 😂 They could have made it look like a normal industrial robot. Instead they named the company after a satyress (a mythical goat-like creature), gave it giant ram's horns, painted it matte black, and then acted surprised when the internet said, "What in the horror movie is THAT?" 😆 Sure, the company says the shape protects sensors and helps it work in dangerous environments. But let's be honest... the dramatic mythological look is also part of the branding. It gets people talking—and judging by all of us arguing about it, it worked. 😄 If I ever need rescuing in the woods and this thing comes walking toward me with glowing eyes... my first thought isn't going to be, "Thank goodness!" It's going to be, "Well... this is one interesting way to meet my maker." 🤣👹🤖
